title: The Secrets of a US Spyware King
gist: In an interview with WIRED, CEO Andrew Boyd says Paragon/REDLattice cannot technically detect customer misuse of its spyware, has no kill switch, and dropped Italy's two contracts on risk grounds without investigating. The $900M acquisition by AE Industrial Partners turned the Israeli spyware firm into a US company on paper, a route around US guardrails on foreign spyware that NSO Group and Candiru then copied. REDLattice plans to go public and is chasing Pentagon, CIA and offensive-cyber contracts.

themes.theme: US ownership as a regulatory end-run

insights.claim: AE Industrial Partners bought Israeli spyware maker Paragon Solutions for $900 million in December 2024 and merged it with REDLattice, its American offensive cyber firm, which this week announced plans to go public.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: An offensive-cyber IPO would give public-market investors direct exposure to commercial spyware, along with its headline risk.
insights.locator: Yet weeks after Paragon, then Israeli-owned

insights.claim: US ownership worked as an end-run around US guardrails on buying foreign spyware: after the AE deal closed, 'everybody started talking' to Paragon, and it began looking to hire 150 new workers.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Changing who owns a firm can open up US government demand for it, a playbook private equity can repeat in defense tech.
insights.quote: Nonetheless, the US acquisition has served as an end-run around foreign-ownership guardrails.
insights.locator: Nonetheless, the US acquisition

insights.claim: Paragon is still effectively Israeli: it keeps its name and offices in Israel with more than 600 employees, and its products still need Israeli government export licensing, while REDLattice products sold abroad fall under US ITAR rules.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Two export-control regimes add regulatory complexity and risk to the combined company's revenue.
insights.quote: The result is a company that is now American on paper, but is still effectively Israeli.
insights.locator: In December 2024, AE acquired it

insights.claim: Boyd says the US government raised no objections and imposed no conditions or governance requirements on the acquisition, though it would never formally approve such a deal.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Informal tolerance rather than formal approval leaves the US government free to change its stance on the deal later.
insights.quote: If the [National Security Council] said, ‘This would be a colossally bad idea,’ we probably wouldn't have gone through with it.
insights.locator: The US government in any form

insights.claim: Within a year, NSO Group and Candiru copied the move: a US investment group took control of NSO and installed former US ambassador to Israel David Friedman as executive chairman, and US-based Integrity Partners acquired Candiru, so all three now compete for US contracts.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: US ownership of Israeli spyware firms is consolidating into a structural trend, with three firms competing for the same US government budgets.
insights.locator: Less than a year after Paragon merged

insights.claim: In 2021 the US sanctioned NSO Group and Candiru and Israel cut the number of countries its firms could sell spyware to from 102 to 37, excluding Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Morocco and Mexico; the US later restricted government purchases of risky foreign spyware.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Regulation squeezed the addressable market of Israeli spyware vendors, which pushed them toward US ownership.
insights.locator: The US Commerce Department sanctioned both

insights.claim: Paragon has no technical way to detect customer misuse because it cannot see whom customers target or what data they extract; it learns of abuse only if customers admit it or third parties such as Citizen Lab uncover it.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Investors cannot rely on the vendor's own controls to limit misuse, so headline and regulatory risk stays high.
insights.locator: More damning, according to critics

insights.claim: Paragon has no kill switch; it can only stop 24-hour support and frequent, essential 'updates', which Boyd says leaves the system ineffective within about 12 hours.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Constant vendor updates create a recurring-revenue dependency and give Paragon de facto leverage to cut off a customer.
insights.quote: Things start falling apart quite quickly,
insights.locator: Paragon also doesn’t have a “kill switch”

insights.claim: Paragon dropped Italy's two intelligence-agency contracts without investigating WhatsApp's allegations, simply because keeping the relationship was 'not worth it, from a risk perspective'; Boyd says this cost seven figures, and Israeli media put the value at tens of millions of dollars.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Spyware vendors will drop customers to protect their reputation, so one allegation can wipe out a large contract.
insights.quote: just was not worth it, from a risk perspective, to maintain the relationship
insights.locator: But Paragon and RedLattice’s new CEO

insights.claim: By its own transparency reports, Paragon has less oversight than NSO Group: NSO claims a kill switch and tamper-proof activity logs that customers must hand over if misuse is alleged, while Paragon logging is optional and the company has no access to it.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: The 'good guy' branding that sets Paragon apart from competitors is weaker than claimed, a reputational risk ahead of an IPO.
insights.locator: But Boyd’s admissions reveal

insights.claim: Boyd presents the lack of log access as a selling point, saying no government would buy tools whose vendor could see sensitive targeting data.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Customer demand for opacity sets a limit on how far the industry can regulate itself.
insights.quote: There's a balancing act between privacy and security and being able to ensure that our customers are using these things correctly
insights.locator: Rather than see Paragon’s lack of access

insights.claim: Citizen Lab's John Scott-Railton argues the admissions show that accountability is bad for business in spyware and that the industry cannot be trusted to regulate itself; he adds that researchers find only a very small subset of infections.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: This argument strengthens the case for binding legislation that could limit spyware vendors' markets.
insights.quote: The CEO admitting that his customers won’t tolerate oversight is refreshing honesty: Accountability is bad for business.
insights.locator: What Paragon is saying in several

insights.claim: Senator Ron Wyden says surveillance tools without oversight are inevitably abused and calls Paragon's refusal to audit how its tool is used a massive red flag.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Congressional scrutiny is a political risk to US spyware contracts and to the planned IPO.
insights.quote: It’s easy to claim your powerful hacking tool isn’t being misused if you go out of your way to ensure you don’t know how customers use it,
insights.locator: US senator Ron Wyden tells WIRED

insights.claim: Boyd cites the single misuse allegation to date as proof that vetting works, but the author notes this ignores how low the odds of detection are, since the spyware is built to avoid discovery.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: A low count of reported misuse is a weak signal, so tail risk of more revelations remains.

insights.claim: Paragon has 20-30 approved countries and more than 100 customers in 23 countries, sells only to national entities in the US and allied countries, and has rejected a 'handful' of countries in the past year.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: These figures size the business: a concentrated government customer base with limited room to add new countries.
insights.locator: Boyd wouldn’t provide a full list

insights.claim: Boyd says vetting 'usually works 99 out of 100 times', and contracts plus a block on targeting +1 US numbers in systems sold abroad are meant to deter abuse in the remaining cases.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: The governance model is preventive rather than detective, which makes the vendor's risk profile dependent on which customers it picks.
insights.locator: The customer vetting, Boyd says

insights.claim: Paragon refuses to sell to Saudi Arabia or any Middle East country, or to post-Maduro Venezuela, yet reportedly signed a Singapore contract worth tens of millions of dollars in 2023.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Applying the vetting criteria selectively exposes contracts in countries with weak press freedom to reputational risk.
insights.locator: They also won’t sell to Venezuela

insights.claim: Under its own criteria (rule of law, corruption, stability), the author asks whether the current Trump administration would pass Paragon's vetting, and Boyd defers allegations of misuse by US customers to inspectors general or Congress.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Concentration in US government sales carries political risk if a domestic misuse scandal emerges.
insights.locator: All of this, of course, leads

insights.claim: Known US contracts are thin: a $2 million Homeland Security Investigations (ICE) contract signed shortly before the acquisition, a DEA contract, and REDLattice's long-standing US Air Force work, though classified contracts would not appear in public records.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: The visible US revenue base is small compared with the $900M price, so the valuation depends on growth that has not yet been shown.
insights.locator: A year after the acquisition, however

insights.claim: Boyd sees the Pentagon, the CIA and the wider national security enterprise as a large unaddressed market for the company's tools.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: This is the core growth thesis for the REDLattice IPO: expanding US defense and intelligence spending on offensive cyber tools.
insights.quote: There are offices across the national security enterprise that don't even know they need our product yet,
insights.locator: A year after the acquisition

insights.claim: REDLattice will pursue the Trump administration's planned contracts for private companies to run offensive cyber operations against cybercriminal groups, even though Boyd says the company currently provides only hardware and software.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Outsourcing offensive cyber operations to private firms is a new procurement category and a source of revenue upside.
insights.locator: In addition to their products

insights.claim: Boyd, a former director of the CIA's Center for Cyber Intelligence who retired in 2023, gives the combined companies government connections, and they now have 5-10 products, up from fewer than five before the merger, including remote 'over-the-horizon' collection tools; REDLattice advertises more than 200 vulnerability researchers.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Ties to intelligence agencies and in-house zero-day research capacity are the company's competitive moat for government contracts.
insights.locator: Boyd, who became CEO of RedLattice

insights.claim: Graphite, Paragon's only publicly identified product, extracts communications from encrypted apps such as WhatsApp and Signal through zero-click zero-day exploits, a narrower scope than NSO's Pegasus, which can take over a phone's microphone and camera.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Commercial exploits threaten encrypted messaging platforms, a security and legal-risk factor for Meta's WhatsApp.
